name: Injection
description: Injection flaws, such as SQL, OS, LDAP, and XPath injection occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The attacker's hostile data can trick the interpreter into executing unintended commands or accessing data without proper authorization.
preventions: Use a safe API which avoids the use of the interpreter entirely or provides a parameterized interface.
If a parameterized API is not available, you should carefully escape special characters using the specific escape syntax for that interpreter.
Positive or 'allow list' input validation is also recommended, but is not a complete defense.

name: Broken Authentication and Session Management
description: Application functions related to authentication and session management are often not implemented correctly, allowing attackers to compromise passwords, keys, or session tokens, or to exploit other implementation flaws to assume other users' identities.
preventions: Meet all the authentication and session management requirements defined in OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS).
Use a single set of strong authentication and session management controls.
Ensure that passwords are at minimum 8 characters and require mixed case, numbers, and special characters.

name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: XSS flaws occur whenever an application takes untrusted data and sends it to a web browser without proper validation or escaping. XSS allows attackers to execute scripts in the victim's browser, which can hijack user sessions, deface web sites, or redirect the user to malicious sites.
preventions: Encode all untrusted data based on the HTML context it is placed in.
Use a positive or allow-list input validation approach.
Apply Content-Security-Policy headers.

name: Insecure Direct Object References
description: A direct object reference occurs when a developer exposes a reference to an internal implementation object, such as a file, directory, or database record. Without an access control check or other protection, attackers can manipulate these references to access unauthorized data.
preventions: Use per user or per session indirect object references.
Check access to the resource each time the application accesses that resource.

name: Security Misconfiguration
description: Good security requires having a secure configuration defined and deployed for the application, frameworks, application server, web server, database server, and platform. Secure settings should be defined, implemented, and maintained, as defaults are often insecure.
preventions: A repeatable hardening process that makes it fast and easy to deploy properly locked-down environments.
Ensure all software is up to date including all code libraries used by the application.
A strong application architecture that provides effective, secure separation between components.

name: Sensitive Data Exposure
description: Many web applications do not properly protect sensitive data, such as credit cards, tax IDs, and authentication credentials. Attackers may steal or modify such weakly protected data to conduct credit card fraud, identity theft, or other crimes. Sensitive data deserves extra protection.
preventions: Classify data processed, stored, or transmitted by an application.
Apply controls as per the classification.
Don't store sensitive data unnecessarily.

name: Missing Function Level Access Control
description: Most web applications verify function level access rights before making that functionality visible in the UI. However, applications need to perform the same access control checks on the server when each function is accessed. If requests are not verified, attackers will be able to forge requests to access functionality without proper authorization.
preventions: Think about the processes that meet the requirements of the application and use them to implement the right controls.
By default, deny all access and require explicit grants.
Check for proper authorization in server-side code.

name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
description: A CSRF attack forces a logged-on victim's browser to send a forged HTTP request, including the victim's session cookie and any other automatically included authentication information, to a vulnerable web application. This allows the attacker to force the victim's browser to generate requests the vulnerable application thinks are legitimate requests from the victim.
preventions: Include a unique, secret, unpredictable token in all state-modifying requests.
Verify the token is correct when the request is received.
For highly sensitive operations, require re-authentication.

name: Using Known Vulnerable Components
description: Components, such as libraries, frameworks, and other software modules, almost always run with full privileges. If a vulnerable component is exploited, such an attack can facilitate serious data loss or server takeover. Applications using components with known vulnerabilities may undermine application defenses.
preventions: Identify all components and the versions you are using, including all dependencies.
Keep components up to date.
Establish security policies governing component use.

name: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards
description: Web applications frequently redirect and forward users to other pages and websites, and use untrusted data to determine the destination pages. Without proper validation, attackers can redirect victims to phishing or malware sites, or use forwards to access unauthorized pages.
preventions: Simply avoid using redirects and forwards.
If used, don't involve user parameters in calculating the destination.
If destination parameters can't be avoided, ensure the supplied value is valid and authorized for the user.
